title: From care to transformation: University teachers' conceptions of caring and excellent teaching
abstract: Abstract This phenomenographic study explores the qualitatively different ways university teachers conceptualise the relationship between care and teaching excellence in higher education (HE). Drawing on interviews and teaching narratives from 21 award‐winning or award‐nominated academics in Hong Kong and the United Kingdom, five hierarchical categories of description were identified and organised within an outcome space: (1) care as necessary but not sufficient for excellence; (2) care and excellence as distinct; (3) care as holistic, relational and student‐centred practice; (4) care as sustaining professional practice; and (5) care as empowerment and transformation. The findings demonstrate that care is not uniformly understood, or conceptualised, by academics but is experienced in qualitatively different ways that vary in inclusiveness. A key contribution of this paper is the identification of ‘sustaining care’ as a distinct conception linking emotional labour, professional boundaries, self‐care and teaching excellence. title: Household worklessness, educational capital and NEET status among young adults in the UK
abstract: Abstract This article examines how household worklessness and educational capital are jointly associated with being not in education, employment or training (NEET) among young adults in the United Kingdom. Existing research often treats educational trajectories and household disadvantage as separate explanatory domains, obscuring how they coexist during the transition to adulthood. Using UK Labour Force Survey household microdata for October–December 2025, the study analyses 5251 people aged 18–24; household‐file‐weighted linked ordinal and logistic regression models are estimated on 5118 complete cases. To prevent definitional overlap between predictor and outcome, household worklessness is constructed from the employment status of other adults, excluding the focal respondent. Compared with working household contexts, workless contexts were associated with substantially higher adjusted odds of NEET (OR = 3.079, 95% CI [2.238, 4.235]). Higher qualifications and recent learning were associated with lower NEET odds, although recent learning did not materially attenuate the household gradient. title: The bright and dark sides of AI in learning: How AI ‐driven challenge and hindrance technostressors affect undergraduate students' academic performance
abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into university learning environments has fundamentally reshaped how undergraduate students access information, complete academic tasks and engage with course content. While AI technologies promise enhanced learning efficiency and personalised support, they also introduce new forms of technostress that may either facilitate or hinder academic performance. Drawing on the challenge–hindrance stressor framework and the Job Demands–Resources (JD‐R) model, this study distinguishes between AI‐driven challenge technostressors (AICS) and AI‐driven hindrance technostressors (AIHS) to examine their differential effects on undergraduate students' academic performance. We further investigate how traditional support structures and peer support structures moderate these relationships. Using longitudinal survey data collected from 391 undergraduate students with AI‐supported learning experience, the results reveal that AICS positively influences academic performance, whereas AIHS exerts a negative effect. title: Observed teacher collaboration indices: Professional learning impact, self‐efficacy and job satisfaction among lower and upper secondary teachers in TALIS 2024
abstract: Abstract Teacher collaboration is widely promoted as a resource for professional learning, teacher efficacy and retention, but research and policy often treat collaboration as a single practice and use frequency as a proxy for professional value. This risks overlooking differences between routine exchange, coordination and deeper forms of collaborative inquiry. Using TALIS 2024 teacher data from eight education systems with both lower and upper secondary participation ( N = 33,137), this study examines how two content‐defined observed practice indices—practice‐focused and exchange/coordination—are associated with perceived professional learning impact, teaching self‐efficacy and job satisfaction. Teacher‐weighted controlled path models with country fixed effects and school‐cluster robust standard errors were estimated. A formal within‐model contrast showed that the practice‐focused index had a larger standardised association with perceived professional learning impact than the exchange/coordination index. title: The ecology of inclusive education reimagined: A framework for research, policy, and practice
abstract: Abstract Evidence suggests the educational gap between those who experience success at school and those who do not is growing. Decades of rhetoric, policy and reform have failed to deliver an inclusive form of schooling that meets the learning needs of all students and much of the blame for this is placed at the feet of schools. The Ecology of inclusive education (Anderson, J., Boyle, C., & Deppeler, J., Equality in education , 2014; pp. 23–34) was conceptualised to guide a study interrogating leadership for inclusive education within the messiness of schools. Semi‐structured qualitative interviews were conducted with seven primary school principals in Queensland, Australia. Inductive thematic analysis of the data yielded some unexpected findings. It exposed the significant influence that both education systems and school communities have on the work of school leaders. Six themes emerged related to systemic influence and included perceiving inclusive education as a continuum and the use of a rhetoric of difference. title: Covering the gaps: Teaching assistants, lesson cover, workforce pressure and displaced support in mainstream schools
abstract: Abstract This article examines the deployment of teaching assistants (TAs) to cover classes in place of teachers in mainstream schools. Drawing on survey data from over 8000 support staff in England, the analysis focuses on the scale, character, reported reasons and consequences of TA‐led cover. The article conceptualises lesson cover as a site through which wider workforce pressures are absorbed and redistributed within schools. It uses the concept of ‘organisational triage’ to describe how schools allocate limited staffing capacity to immediate and visible demands under constrained conditions. The findings suggest that TA‐led cover is common and often substantial: two‐thirds of TAs reported covering classes as part of their role, and among those who covered on their most recent working day, the estimated mean duration was 2 h 41 min. Reported reasons for cover included planned release, short‐term absence and wider staffing pressures, including unfilled vacancies and shortages of usual cover staff. title: Climate assemblies involving children and youth as socio‐educational spaces: Perceived success factors, challenges and opportunities
abstract: Abstract Climate assemblies have emerged as participatory mechanisms and as socio‐educational spaces for engaging citizens in climate decision‐making and promoting sustainability learning. However, to date, initiatives involving children and young people remain underexplored. This study investigates the implementation of climate assemblies involving children and youth in the United Kingdom, focusing on the perceived success factors and conditions that enable meaningful participation and learning, as well as the challenges and opportunities that emerge when developing deliberative democratic processes with younger participants. The research adopts an exploratory qualitative design based on interviews with 14 leaders and key agents involved in 11 climate assembly initiatives across community, local authority and school contexts. Findings indicate that the perceived success of these initiatives depends on a combination of structural, relational and institutional factors. Sustained funding, long‐term partnerships, flexible facilitation and inclusive design were identified as essential for supporting participation beyond one‐off engagement activities. title: Reconfiguring thinking through ChatGPT ‐mediated learning: Metacognition, engagement and cognitive agency in a youth apprenticeship programme
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted as a means of supporting learning, metacognition and self‐regulated learning. However, less is known about how thinking is reconfigured through generative AI‐mediated learning and how these processes unfold within particular pedagogical and social conditions. This qualitative study examines how students' thinking practices, learning processes and cognitive agency are reconfigured through ChatGPT‐mediated learning within a youth apprenticeship programme in the United States. Guided by distributed cognition and learning ecology, the study employed an interpretive multi‐perspectival design drawing on semi‐structured interviews, approximately 300 h of classroom observations, ethnographic conversations and student‐generated artefacts. Reflexive thematic analysis indicated that thinking emerged through iterative interactions among learners, AI, peers and instructional contexts. Students' engagement varied according to the pedagogical and social conditions surrounding AI use, while cognitive agency was enacted through continual judgements about credibility, authorship and responsibility for AI‐generated knowledge. title: How curriculum modifications shape educational pathways: Evidence from linked administrative data in Switzerland
abstract: Abstract The increasing heterogeneity of learning needs and preconditions in inclusive mainstream classrooms entails that not all learners are equally able to meet the regular learning objectives. In response, various integrative measures have been implemented to tailor instruction to students' individual needs. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how such measures shape students' subsequent educational pathways. The present study focuses on curriculum modifications, a measure for low‐achieving students that entails individualised adaptations of learning objectives, and examines their association with educational pathways in secondary education, using Switzerland as a case study. Drawing on stigma and signalling theories, the study investigates whether receiving curriculum modifications is linked to differential educational trajectories. The analysis is based on large‐scale, administratively linked test score data from four Swiss cantons and employs a propensity score matching approach to account for the multidimensional differences between students who received curriculum modifications and those who did not. title: From individual to collective: Post‐return agency among internationally educated Mongolian graduates
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how internationally educated Mongolian graduates pursue professional projects after returning to Mongolian higher education and how some of these projects develop from individual academic agency into collective action. It draws on semi‐structured interviews with 30 graduates trained in Japan, South Korea, China, Taiwan, Germany, Czech, Hungary, the United Kingdom and the United States, across engineering and technology, agriculture, natural sciences, health and medical sciences, social sciences and humanities. The findings identify a layered pattern of post‐return agency. Graduates first repositioned themselves as ‘local experts with international experience’ and adapted their teaching, research and professional expectations to local conditions. Some then coordinated through departmental relationships, while a smaller subset built institutional, professional and transnational alliances. The clearest collective initiatives were found among seven participants. Arab teachers' understandings of the ethical code of teaching in Israel
abstract: Abstract Professional codes of ethics are essential for guiding teachers' moral responsibilities, yet Israel has no established ethical code for the profession—particularly within its Arab education system, which operates under complex socio‐political conditions. This qualitative multiple‐case study explored how 14 experienced Arab teachers in Israel understand the purposes, meanings and obstacles related to applying a professional ethical code in their schools. Semi‐structured interviews revealed that teachers conceptualize professional ethics through multiple frameworks: deontology (Kantian ethics) and virtue ethics underpin their commitment to teaching as a ‘higher calling’; care ethics, virtue ethics and social justice ethics shape their relationships with students; and care ethics alongside Kantian principles guide collegial interactions. However, participants identified significant barriers. They criticized the dominance of utilitarian, outcome‐based education that marginalizes values education and reduces teaching to measurable metrics. title: Occupational recognition and teachers’ retention intentions: A latent profile analysis informed by recognition theory
abstract: Abstract Teacher retention is often explained through workload, job satisfaction and burnout, but these accounts have examined less systematically whether teachers experience their profession as socially and institutionally recognised. Drawing on recognition theory, this study examines how occupational recognition is configured across material and employment conditions, proximal relationships and societal‐policy status, and how these configurations are associated with retention‐related intentions. Using IBM SPSS Statistics and Mplus, we analysed weighted responses from 2686 lower secondary teachers in Shanghai, China, from the Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024. Latent profile analysis used three theory‐derived composites. Manual Bolck‐Croon‐Hagenaars analyses compared profiles on wished years to continue teaching and five possible reasons for leaving, adjusting primarily for age group and using total teaching experience as a sensitivity covariate. A three‐profile solution comprising low (12.4%), moderate (70.2%) and high (17.4%) recognition profiles was the most stable and interpretable. title: Incorporating student voice in curriculum design to Foster high school students' motivation: Insights from social cognitive theory
abstract: Abstract Although student voice has attracted increasing scholarly attention, earlier research has already indicated that students' participation may enhance curriculum relevance, engagement, youth development, democratic learning and school improvement. Yet, how high school students experience curriculum‐level voice as a motivational process shaped through the reciprocal personal, environmental and behavioural dimensions of Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) remains less clearly understood. For this reason, the present study examined how student voice in curriculum design might influence high school students' motivation from the perspective of SCT. Drawing upon a qualitative approach, 28 high school students completed reflective written forms describing their perceptions. The data were analysed phenomenographically to identify the major categories and themes. The findings suggested three main categories: personal factors, including increased self‐efficacy, ownership and alignment with personal goals; environmental factors, including supportive teacher‐student relationships, culturally responsive curriculum and institutional support; and behavioural factors, including active engagement,

title: From liquid learning to weaving learning: Negotiating meanings of Children's learning in family travel
abstract: Abstract Children's learning increasingly extends into everyday informal settings, but what counts as learning in these contexts remains insufficiently understood. Focusing on family travel as a mobile and socioculturally situated informal learning context, this study adopts a sociocultural perspective and uses liquid learning as a sensitising concept to examine how Chinese families negotiate meanings of children's learning. Using a whole‐family design with child‐centred methods, the study involved 10 children aged 7–12 and their parents across the pre‐, during‐ and post‐travel phases. Findings reveal cognitive, affective, and embodied meanings of learning. The sociocultural shaping of these meanings is conceptualised as weaving learning , a process through which families negotiate competing purposes shaped by both the contemporary conditions of change and uncertainty (as captured by liquid learning) and the Chinese sociocultural context. This study advances educational research by foregrounding how travel experiences become understood and valued as learning, and extends liquid learning by showing how the liquidity of learning is unevenly realised through sociocultural negotiation.

title: ‘More than information’: A social listening and platform architecture analysis of online special educational needs and disabilities discourse
abstract: Abstract Parents of children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) increasingly seek information and support through online discussions, yet little is known about how architectural features of digital platforms shape the interactions and support that parents encounter. The paper makes two contributions: First, it develops and applies a transferable social listening framework that integrates manual qualitative collection with automated application programming interface capture, topic modelling and discourse network analysis; second, it demonstrates how platform architecture shapes the forms of interaction and support that emerge across online SEND communities. Data were collected over a 12‐month period across three platforms: Mumsnet, Facebook and Instagram, yielding 3312 posts and 19,349 interactions. Topic modelling and clustering identified thematic groupings, while discourse network visualisation revealed distinctive patterns of interaction between the platforms. Facebook and Instagram were dominated by informational and promotional content, including news, services and job opportunities, with relatively limited discussion between users. A beacon of inclusion for our whole community: Examining a civic university through the lens of LGBTQ + inclusion
abstract: Abstract This exploratory article explores how one UK university sought to understand and enhance its engagement with the local LGBTQ+ community. Drawing on poststructuralist queer and homonormative theories and civic university frameworks, the study analyses data from a community‐facing Pride survey completed by 53 LGBTQ+ individuals. Through emergent coding and thematic analysis, eight key issues are identified: experiences of marginalisation, visibility and community engagement, safe and inclusive spaces, support services, outreach, inclusive institutional values, LGBTQ+ learning opportunities and the need for community connection. The findings highlight the persistence of cis and heteronormativity and the importance of universities as sites of refuge, affirmation, inclusion and resistance. This study shows that LGBTQ+ individuals look to their local university not only as an educational provider but also as an ethical leader, a support network and a cultural anchor. As an exploratory study, these findings are intended to provide indicative insights into how universities are perceived, rather than generalisable conclusions about institutional practice. title: Music education in British schools: The relationship between music education, cognitive skills and perceived academic outcomes
abstract: Abstract In recent years, there has been increased attention on the effect of extracurricular activities on the academic performance of students, especially in the music education (ME) programme. The study aimed to analyse the relationship between participation in the ME programme and the academic performance of learners between 6 and 17 years. A quantitative survey design was used to collect data from 420 students in three British international schools in China through self‐report questionnaires that examined students' perceptions of ME participation, learning experiences and skill development. ME participation was positively associated with cognitive skills, academic engagement and self‐regulation skills. In turn, cognitive skills, academic engagement and self‐regulation skills were positively associated with perceived academic outcomes. Mediation analysis further indicated that these factors significantly explained the relationship between ME participation and perceived academic outcomes. title: Looking for hopeful purpose in England's environmental education policy: An analysis of the National Education Nature Park
abstract: Abstract The intertwined crises of climate change, biodiversity loss and environmental degradation represent profound global challenges. Education holds a unique role in enabling all young people to navigate uncertainty, participate meaningfully in decision‐making and contribute to more just and sustainable ways of living. In 2022, the Department for Education in England published a sustainability and climate change strategy which included the National Education Nature Park (NENP) programme. Using Carol Bacchi's ‘What's the Problem Represented to Be?’ (WPR) approach, we examined the first two years of the implementation of the NENP, analysing published materials ( n = 20) to consider how the purposes of Environmental Education are understood, constructed and implemented. We identified three broad themes: (1) Science and/or STEM knowledge and skills are fundamental to engagement with nature, (2) Measurement is the ‘signature pedagogy’ of the NENP and (3) Nature Connectedness is broadly understood as individual and linked to personal wellbeing. title: Inclusive climate pedagogy in low‐resource schooling contexts: A context‐responsive framework for access, participation and learning equity across climate‐vulnerable education systems
abstract: Abstract This qualitative multiple‐case study examines how teachers and school leaders enact inclusive climate pedagogy in low‐resource, climate‐vulnerable public secondary schools in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews ( n = 16), 24 h of classroom observations and document review, the Context‐Responsive Inclusive Climate Education Framework (CRICEF) was developed to explain how access, participation and learning equity are co‐produced through interactions among structural constraints, pedagogical agency and relational leadership. Findings show (1) emergent teacher‐driven pedagogical principles (ethical inclusivity; place‐based contextualisation; pedagogical flexibility; relational responsiveness); (2) structural barriers (assessment pressures, material scarcity, policy incoherence) which normalise climate disruption; and (3) leadership as a central mediating domain enabling or constraining inclusive practice. The paper argues for curriculum, teacher development and governance reforms that treat climate vulnerability as a routine condition for inclusion. Implications for policy and school‐level practice are discussed.

title: The epistemic ceiling: Veteran practitioners' perspectives on primary qualification entry standards for teaching secondary mathematics in Scotland
abstract: Abstract This paper presents an exploratory analysis of contemporary curricular and professional qualification policies in the Scottish education system, focusing on minimum qualification thresholds for mathematics teaching. The study examines how veteran secondary mathematics practitioners perceive the structural and pedagogical implications of using an SCQF Level 5 qualification baseline for primary and out‐of‐field educators within the Broad General Education. Grounded in Michael Young's ‘powerful knowledge’ paradigm and the Three Futures framework, the paper analyses systemic tensions between educational genericism and disciplinary mastery. Adopting an interpretivist framework, the study employs Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA) to evaluate qualitative data drawn from the asynchronous written reflections of a purposive cohort of six veteran secondary mathematics teachers. The analysis indicates that participants view the lower qualification ceiling as institutionalising an instrumental approach that disconnects early secondary curricula from formal abstract structures, such as algebra and deductive proof. title: Educational philosophising in the Everyday : UK immigrant mothers navigating identity and praxis during COVID ‐19
abstract: Abstract Debates surrounding motherhood have long centred on women's roles as carers. Although motherhood is now more widely recognised within feminist scholarship, it often remains conceptually separate from identities associated with formal educational discourse. Yet mothers frequently act not only as facilitators of learning but also as reflective actors who shape how education is understood and practised in everyday life. This paper engages with these debates to argue that, while mothers undertake care work, they also participate in the facilitation and interpretation of knowledge, engaging with their children's learning at a deeper, reflective level. Drawing on the work of Bell Hooks and Richard Pring, we suggest that mothers may be understood as informal education providers who facilitate holistic learning experiences for their children. At the same time, their everyday engagement with children's education involves reflective interpretation and meaning making, which can be understood as a form of philosophising about education. title: Shaping futures from a distance: Joint trajectories of remote parenting and their links to academic outcomes in China's left‐behind youth
abstract: Abstract This longitudinal study explored the distinct trajectories of remote parenting practices as perceived by China's left‐behind middle school students and the associations of these trajectories on academic achievement and resilience. Data were collected from 2981 first‐year middle school students whose parents are migrant workers. Using parallel‐process growth mixture modelling, we identified five distinct trajectories of remote authoritarian parenting and remote parental involvement in learning. The High Stable Remote Involvement with Decline in Remote Authoritarian Parenting trajectory (54.38%) achieved the highest academic performance and academic resilience. Conversely, the Decreasing Remote Involvement with Rising Remote Authoritarian Parenting trajectory (9.39%) showed the lowest outcomes. These findings underscore the critical importance of maintaining consistent and supportive remote parental involvement while reducing controlling behaviours to enhance the academic and psychological well‐being of left‐behind adolescents.

title: The ecology of hope: Building rainbows in education systems
abstract: Abstract Hope is frequently invoked in education, yet rarely theorised. Where it has been theorised, it has been understood in two largely separate ways: as an individual psychological capacity, in the positive‐psychology tradition and as a critical‐emancipatory stance, in the pedagogy of hope. This article proposes a third: a theory, the ecology of hope, that locates hope not in the individual alone but in the relationship between a person and the systems that surround them. Bringing the cognitive psychology of hope into dialogue with ecological systems theory, the social‐ecological account of resilience, and utopian methodology, in which a better society is something deliberately designed, it argues that hope is an emergent and designable property of educational ecologies: something a system can build, a learner can be helped to perceive and may in time learn to seek for themselves. For young people who have experienced adversity, and who often arrive with hesitant hope, or with little hope at all, this cultivation is especially consequential and involves the gradual development of learned hopefulness. title: ‘In a small school, it's just capacity all of the time’: Delivery and experiences of a national early career teacher development initiative across diverse school settings in England
abstract: Abstract Effective early career support is associated with a variety of professional and personal benefits for teachers and their schools. However, research indicates that the contextual features of schools, such as their size and geographic location, influence the support that new teachers receive. This mixed‐methods study explores an initiative for the support and development of new teachers in England, the ‘Early Career Framework’ (ECF), as a case study to examine links between early career teacher support and school context. Drawing on ecological perspectives and conceptual approaches for addressing wicked problems, we employed a predominantly qualitative mixed‐methods design, combining semi‐structured interviews with 17 participants and a mixed‐methods survey across 68 schools. Building on prior cross‐context evaluations, we examined the factors that supported effective delivery and positive experiences of the ECF across diverse school contexts in England, focusing particularly on small schools and those in rural and coastal settings. title: The reasons behind the resources: Understanding the beliefs that shape lecturers' educational curation
abstract: Abstract This study explores lecturers' educational curation, that is: how they select, structure and share educational resources, and how this curational behaviour is shaped by their beliefs. Semi‐structured interviews with 23 lecturers at a Dutch University of Applied Sciences show that curational behaviour comprises five curational activities: searching for resources, assessing and selecting resources, creating and editing resources, structuring resources and sharing resources. These are complemented by the meta‐activity of soliciting feedback. The findings illustrate how these curational activities are shaped by a diverse and personal mix of behavioural, normative and control beliefs. Lecturers emphasized the activities of searching for resources and subsequently assessing and selecting them, and for this, mainly considered content‐focused beliefs about student learning outcomes, quality of resources and resource availability. This may reflect the nature of curation: even within student‐focused approaches of education, lecturers believe that learning requires a foundation of appropriate content, leading to content‐focused beliefs being particularly salient. title: Issue Information
Change fatigue, teacher exhaustion and work engagement: The buffering role of transformational leadership
abstract: Abstract Although constant changes driven by reforms, technological adaptations and shifts in formal rules and regulations have contributed to the emergence of change fatigue in education, the consequences and mitigating factors remain largely underexplored. This study examined the extent to which change fatigue was related to teacher emotional exhaustion and work engagement in Türkiye. Additionally, it examined transformational leadership as a buffering mechanism in the relationship between change fatigue, exhaustion and engagement. Data were collected from 516 teachers and analysed using structural equation modelling. Findings revealed that perceived change fatigue was significantly associated with emotional exhaustion, which in turn was negatively associated with work engagement. The relationship between change fatigue and work engagement was rather indirect, with emotional exhaustion as the mediator. Furthermore, transformational leadership played a protective role by weakening the negative link between exhaustion and engagement, but not the relationship between change fatigue and emotional exhaustion. title: Bricks, knots, and bodies: Material encounters and the affective making of masculinity
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how creative research methods do not just capture boys' experiences of masculinity, but actively materialise them. Drawing on two arts‐based activities used in school‐based fieldwork (a mannequin‐based exercise with one participant and a Lego‐building workshop with a small peer group), the paper analyses how materials generate different affective conditions for the making of masculinity. Rather than treating arts‐based methods as conduits to boys' ‘voices’, the paper approaches them as affective apparatuses (Barad, 2007) that shape the rhythms, atmospheres and orientations through which masculinity becomes legible and inhabitable. The mannequin offered a surface for revision and accumulation, enabling masculinity to be reworked slowly and affectively over time. Labels slipped, overlapped and were crossed out; meaning was continually re/opened. In contrast, the Lego session produced solidity and grievance, where masculinity was crystallised in relation to threat and power shifts. title: Governance of generative AI in higher education: A qualitative analysis of universities' policies and global insights
abstract: Abstract As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated into higher education, institutions face challenges in balancing its benefits with potential risks, including plagiarism, misinformation, bias and privacy concerns. This study examines the policies and guidelines on generative AI usage implemented by leading US universities ranking based best colleges in the world in the US News List using a qualitative document analysis approach. The study identifies key themes in generative AI governance, including responsible experimentation, transparency, AI literacy and faculty discretion in policy implementation. While universities recognise the potential of AI to enhance learning and research, policies vary significantly across regions, with European institutions adhering to stricter regulations and US universities granting faculty greater flexibility. The results also provide valuable insights for policymakers and educators seeking to develop responsible AI governance frameworks in higher education.

title: Digital wellbeing education for adolescents: A conceptual framework
abstract: Abstract As digital media and technologies become increasingly integral to adolescents' daily lives, it is important that young people develop the knowledge and skills needed not only to navigate digital environments, but also to do so in ways that enhance, maintain and protect their wellbeing. Concurrent rises in adolescent digital engagement and declining mental health and wellbeing make this an urgent educational priority. This article introduces digital wellbeing education —the integrated development of knowledge and skills needed to navigate digital environments in ways conducive to wellbeing—as a distinct objective within compulsory secondary schooling. Existing educational approaches, including digital literacy, digital citizenship and socio–emotional learning provide an important foundation for digital wellbeing education but remain conceptually fragmented, with digital wellbeing under‐theorised as an explicit educational goal. Integrating these traditions, we propose a novel competency‐based framework comprising three domains: (1) functional, (2) critical and (3) social–emotional, emphasising the importance of their integrated and applied development through education. title: Bourdieu in Aotearoa New Zealand: A systematic review of theoretical applications in educational research, 2000–2025
abstract: Abstract This article presents the first systematic review of scholarship applying Pierre Bourdieu's theoretical framework in New Zealand educational research, drawing on 30 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, studies were coded for Bourdieusian concepts applied, depth of theoretical application (descriptive, explanatory or generative), theoretical engagement depth and whether authors explicitly acknowledged tension between Bourdieu's framework and New Zealand's settler‐colonial, bicultural educational context. The findings reveal that capital is applied in 97% of studies, habitus in 93% and field in 87%; secondary concepts (symbolic violence, doxa, logic of practice and misrecognition) each appear in fewer than 30% of the corpus. The dominant mode of application is explanatory rather than generative, with only six studies (20%) proposing new theoretical constructs or generative extensions of Bourdieu's framework. Eleven studies (37%) acknowledge theoretical friction with New Zealand's bicultural educational context, and no early childhood education study met the criteria for inclusion in the corpus. title: Flourishing through adventure learning: A (semi)cautionary tale
abstract: Abstract Studies suggest that adventure learning can develop children's cognitive skills and promote social and emotional learning. However, evidence is needed as to whether the design of adventure learning—school‐based or external/residential—plays a role in that development/promotion, and whether learning gains are maintained. This paper reports the findings of a large‐scale randomised controlled trial with a synergic implementation process evaluation. Randomisation was at the school level. The trial was carried out in 97 schools in the United Kingdom with children aged 11–12. We investigated two different approaches to adventure learning delivery (5‐day school‐based and 5‐day residential) and the longer‐term impacts. The short‐term impact was assessed immediately after the intervention. The long‐term impact was assessed after 8 months. Data revealed that both programmes had a positive short‐term impact on student engagement and self‐regulation but limited longer‐term impact on student engagement and behaviour. title: Breaking point: Identifying the factors that predict suspension from school
abstract: Abstract School suspensions are associated with adverse educational and psychosocial outcomes, yet little is known about how structural disadvantage, relational factors, health behaviours, well‐being indicators and school‐level factors jointly predict suspension risk in England. To our knowledge, this is the first study in England to model structural, relational, health‐behaviour, well‐being and school‐level predictors of suspension simultaneously within a single ecological framework. We draw on linked psychosocial survey and administrative data and separately estimate predictors of initial suspension and of repeated suspension. The study extends a literature dominated by demographic analyses of national administrative data and provides evidence for both established and previously underexamined associations. We analysed #BeeWell survey and linked administrative suspension data from pupils aged 12–15 across Hampshire and Southampton ( N = 19,064, attending 69 secondary schools). Bayesian zero‐inflated negative binomial regression was used to model both the likelihood of receiving at least one suspension and the frequency of suspensions among those suspended. title: Exploring interactions of the dimensions of agency through the experiences of aspiring school leaders in Scotland, UK
abstract: Abstract Agency has increasingly become a central concept in educational leadership research, yet its application to those preparing to enter school leadership roles remains underexplored. Drawing on the conceptual framework of the ecological approach to teacher agency, we explored how and in what ways aspiring school leaders in Scotland ( n = 21) experience agency as they undertake a national programme of professional learning designed to support their entry into school leadership— Into Headship . Drawing on data gathered from critical incidents ( n = 56) provided by the school leaders and written during their completion of the Into Headship programme during 2021–2024, we explored the ways in which the different dimensions of agency were visible and how they interact. We found a strong presence of the cultural and structural aspect of the practical‐evaluative dimension of agency and evident interactions between the practical‐evaluative, iterative and projective dimensions of agency. We also noted how aspiring school leaders identify and create spaces of agency for others. title: Exploring the early observations of parents supporting their children with school attendance problems ( SAPs ): A co‐produced study
abstract: Abstract School Attendance Problems (SAPs) represent a significant challenge requiring early identification and intervention. Current service provision often does not recognise early indicators that parents observe, creating gaps between when initial concerns are raised and formal support is provided. This paper presents an explorative study on early indicators of SAPs focusing on the lived experiences of parents in post‐pandemic England. The paper details the parental perspectives on what constitutes early signs of SAPs, suggesting the need for parent‐school collaboration in addressing these difficulties before they become established. This study was exploratory in design. A co‐produced survey was employed to capture authentic parent experiences of SAPs. The section of the questionnaire analysed in this paper focuses on the identification of early indicators of SAPs. Polyvagal Theory (PVT) was utilised as an analytical framework, which suggests that underlying attendance challenges can be linked with autonomic nervous system responses to environments perceived as unsafe. title: The critical role of teacher educators in promoting socially just mathematics teaching
abstract: Abstract This paper focuses on the enablers and constraints that shape mathematics teacher educators' agency in addressing social justice issues within their practice and how these can be harnessed or overcome. Given the potential impact of teacher educators on the student/practising teachers they work with, and consequently on the agency of classroom teachers in teaching for social justice, this is an important area that warrants further research. We adopted a participatory action research methodology in establishing a team of 15 ‘teacher educators’ (broadly defined) working in universities and other settings across England and Scotland. We drew on a theoretical framework based on critical pedagogy and critical mathematics education. Research team meetings focused on designing and evaluating teaching strategies and professional development workshops, which were tried out with student teachers and practising teachers. Data were collected from group discussions in which teacher educators reflected on constraints and opportunities within their own practice. title: More‐than‐gender? Moving beyond gendered expectations of divergent learners in early childhood education
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we explore how neurodivergent ways of being in early education are often gendered. The intersectionalities of gender and neurodivergence often lead to fixed expectations that perpetuate binary interpretations, pathologisations, missed diagnoses and a lack of curated support. Girls tend to be schooled from a young age in performing socially acceptable roles that delineate them as ‘good’ girls. Yet normative expectations can be highly challenging for girls' bodies and brains labelled ‘neurodivergent’ because they function differently. We argue that all divergent bodies desire/require space for sensory‐kinaesthetic‐movement‐haptic‐cognitive experiences to function well. The paper shares two stories of young girls in UK settings who don't speak. Each ‘neurodivergent’ storying resists expectations of how a body should be within oppressive learning systems that regulate according to gendered rules. Extending our PhD research, we trouble traditional figurations of ‘girl’ and suggest alternative ways educators might teach‐care for them. title: ‘I was treated as a deficit’: Immigrant teachers' career progression in Australia
abstract: Abstract Immigrant teachers have long been recruited through skilled and employer‐sponsored migration schemes to address teacher shortages in Australia, yet their career trajectories remain constrained by systemic inequities that limit their integration and professional development opportunities. Using a Longitudinal Interpretative Phenomenological Approach (LIPA), this study examines immigrant teachers' lived experiences of career progression within the Australian education system through the lens of Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT). Data were collected from the three rounds of semi‐structured interviews with a group of eight immigrant teachers in New South Wales, Australia across two academic years. This study found that immigrant teachers' career development unfolds through recurring cycles of disillusionment, adaptation and cautious re‐engagement, shaped by the interplay of schools' relational dynamics, institutional and structural constraints and life‐domain resources. Rather than having systemic support, their career progression of immigrant teachers often hinges on uneven access to supportive school environments, individual effort and compensatory resources from broader

title: Powerful transformations: The experiences of higher education teaching staff who were first‐generation university students
abstract: Abstract Historically, a university education has been seen primarily as a route for the middle classes to achieve professional qualifications while structural barriers have served to restrict entry to individuals from particular demographics. First‐generation students (FGS), often with low socio‐economic backgrounds, face multiple barriers to Higher Education (HE) and are less likely than their more advantaged peers to apply, be accepted or to complete their studies. FGS who become HE lecturers are examples of those who were able to overcome their disadvantages and who, by choosing to stay within academia, demonstrate successful assimilation into a university setting. Examination of the experiences and perspectives of HE lecturers who had been FGS provides an opportunity to understand the factors that supported the retention of these individuals in HE and could inform recommendations for future widening participation strategies. This study utilised an online qualitative survey to explore the experiences of 14 teaching staff in HE who had been FGS. Participants were invited to reflect on their time as a student and how this influenced their teaching practices. Data were thematicall

title: Lessons from local area special educational needs and disability inspections: A content analysis of Ofsted and Care Quality Commission outcome letters
abstract: Abstract The growing concern about demand for, and provision of, support for children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) has led the English government to announce a review of the system, which many describe as being in crisis. The Office for Standards in Education, Children's Services and Skills (Ofsted) and the Care Quality Commission inspect local areas to evaluate how they fulfil SEND statutory duties. Findings are published in narrative outcome letters, highlighting strengths and areas for development. Where significant weaknesses are identified, the local area must produce a Written Statement of Action, followed by a revisit. Recent revisits show widespread underperformance. This study synthesised strengths and weaknesses across a representative sample of outcome letters from SEND inspections conducted between 2016 and 2022. Through content analysis, we reviewed 36 initial inspection letters to identify common strengths and areas for development, analysed 34 revisit letters to explore recurring areas of significant weakness and assessed progress in those areas. title: Rethinking quality in Early Childhood Education ( ECE ) from Chinese children's perspectives: Engaging with, resisting and reimagining institutional and social norms
abstract: Abstract While the concept of ‘quality’ in Early Childhood Education (ECE) has been widely theorised, it remains largely shaped by adult‐centric perspectives and globalised frameworks that prioritise standardisation and developmental outcomes. This paper explores how Chinese children understand and experience quality in ECE. By inviting children to respond to the question ‘What is a good kindergarten?’, the study investigates how they interpret quality through their daily experiences, routines and responses to rules and social norms within kindergarten settings. The research involved 64 children aged approximately 6 years from two public kindergartens in two developed Chinese cities. Data were collected through a two‐stage process: individual interviews prompted by children's drawings and group interviews following collaborative block‐building activities. Findings suggest that children construct quality not only through alignment with institutional norms, such as national ceremonies and classroom routines, but also through acts of resistance, emotional expression and imaginative reconstruction of space. title: Beyond literacy interventions: How four secondary schools leverage social capital to raise student outcomes in a remote, rural context in England
abstract: Abstract This article examines how four secondary schools in a remote, rural and coastal region implemented evidence‐based approaches to improve student literacy. It introduces a novel nested capitals framework that integrates social capital theory with professional capital and institutional capital, conceptualising these as interacting across multiple system levels (students and families, staff and schools). We analyse how leaders and teachers in the case study schools mobilised and aligned these forms of capital in their efforts to enhance literacy outcomes. Findings reveal broad similarities in the implementation of the literacy programme, but also adaptations shaped by differences in professional and institutional capital across the four schools. These practices were further shaped by distinct school‐level logics in relation to students' social capital. For example, while the two schools serving more advantaged communities could rely on students' existing social capital, the two serving disadvantaged communities were focused on raising aspirations and broadening students' experience‐base, albeit in different ways. title: Who gets published? Academic status and publication opportunities in leading Chinese and international higher education journals
abstract: Abstract Academic publishing is central to scholarly recognition and career advancement, yet access to publication opportunities remains unevenly distributed. This study examines how academic status shapes publication opportunities in leading Chinese CSSCI and international SSCI higher education journals. Drawing on a mixed‐methods design, the study analyses publication data from six journals (2013–2024) and incorporates semi‐structured interviews with early career researchers (ECRs). The findings reveal clear differences between the two publishing contexts. SSCI journals are generally perceived to follow a more universalistic logic that emphasizes research quality, whereas CSSCI journals display stronger particularistic tendencies. Moreover, academic status significantly shapes publication opportunities, particularly in the Chinese context, contributing to a Matthew Effect in which scholars from prestigious institutions and those with senior titles gain disproportionate publication advantages. Consequently, ECRs, especially those from non‐elite institutions, face intense performance pressures alongside status‐based gatekeeping within the publication process. The study highlights t

title: Children's food activism: Reflections on knowledge and responsibility
abstract: Abstract Children as activists have become more prominent in recent years. Their activism is manifest in relation to conspicuously political topics such as Black Lives Matter, voting rights, being able to air their views or protesting against injustices related to race, culture and other identities. Less often, if at all, do children engage politically with issues related to food. In discussing questions of food activism, this article draws on reflections from the ‘Food activism in the schoolyard’ knowledge exchange project that prompted discussion amongst practitioners working with children across formal and informal education contexts in Scotland. Specifically, the article puts a spotlight on the topic of learning for sustainability to address the question of children's food activism. It does so by highlighting two key considerations that impinge on it being a prominent feature in children's lives educationally and more broadly: children's knowledge (or lack thereof) in relation to food, and the question of whose responsibility it is to be concerned about issues related to food. While food is a key component in school curricula, opportunities for interdisciplinary, cross‐sectoral

title: Special Issue: What place for activism in, for and as education?

What is a curriculum for life? Using youth participatory action research and applied arts to understand and amplify undergraduate students', children's and young people's mental health and wellbeing recommendations for education
abstract: Abstract Mental health is a critical issue globally, with young people being one of the most affected groups. Young people have campaigned vehemently for a ‘curriculum for life,’ arguing that their education is failing to meet their needs (British Council, 2022). The International Survey of Children's Wellbeing reports that children and young people feel adults do not listen to them. As academics working in the Education Department of a University, our research aimed to generate a greater understanding of children and young people's lived experiences of school. Employing youth co‐participatory action research with children (pre‐18) and undergraduate students on education and pre‐service teacher programmes (post‐18), the research aimed to create a greater understanding of their experiences and amplify their recommendations for a more responsive curriculum. Drawing on arts‐based methodologies, the study captured their in‐depth critical reflections through poetry, movement and imagery. Drawing from self‐determination theory, the data reveal four inter‐related themes: seeking connection, mental health, curriculum and powerlessness. title: A repertoire of middle leading practices: A large‐scale investigation of middle leadership in schools
abstract: Abstract This article presents findings from an Australian study investigating the practices of middle leaders responsible for facilitating school development. Despite middle leaders being increasingly recognised as essential in the development of teaching and learning in schools, middle leadership remains under‐researched and comparatively overlooked within the broader educational leadership field. Framed by the theory of practice architectures, which attends to the site‐based conditions which enable and constrain how practices happen, a multimethod, multiphase, multisite study was designed to investigate the practices of middle leaders. Reflexive thematic analysis across five research phases produced five central themes forming what we described as a repertoire of middle leading practices. These broad practices include advocating and negotiating; building productive teams; coordinating, organising and managing; developing teaching practice; and evaluating evidence. Evidence showed that these practices were multifaceted, interdependent and complex and held together by conditions described as ‘threads’. Threads were found in the relational, dialogic and responsive nature of middle

title: Knowing education in Thailand like a global expert organisation: Politics, context and data
abstract: Abstract Global expert organisations play increasingly significant roles in the way that education is understood and governed internationally, including by influencing the discourses through which education is conceptualised and shaping norms of what counts as success, failure, progress and the most desirable visions for the future. By constructing understandings of education in multiple countries globally over extended periods of time, often through large‐scale data generation, they create highly authoritative spaces of knowledge about education. Part of this influence is exerted through regular and substantial written reports about country‐specific issues, progress and futures. This paper examines how education in Thailand comes to be known through global expert organisations by critically analysing a selection of reports on education in Thailand from 1999 to 2024. We argue that these reports produce distinctive ways of knowing that are de‐politicised, de‐contextualised and heavily shaped by large‐scale international comparative data. We examine these knowledge practices through the conceptual lenses of time, scale and certainty. We conclude with a set of practical recommendation

title: When rhythm speaks: Exploring linguistic identity in Saudi Arabia's kindergarten Auditory Arts Program
abstract: Abstract This study explores the role of auditory arts—particularly music, rhythm and sound‐based activities—in shaping linguistic identity within Saudi Arabian early childhood education (ECE). Grounded in the philosophical insights of Al‐Farabi and the contemporary framework of Gert Biesta's World‐Centred Education theory, the research examines how audio–musical experiences support children's linguistic, cognitive, social and aesthetic development. Using a qualitative descriptive design, the study employed two methods: (1) focus group discussions with 12 trained early‐childhood teachers; and (2) a conceptual content analysis of the national Teachers' Guide for Auditory Arts Activities for KG3. Findings from the content analysis revealed three overarching themes—the competency pulse, the social cadence and the self in motion—with a strong dominance of cognitive and linguistic skills across all units, while social, cultural and creative components appeared less frequently. Focus group findings reinforced the guide's emphasis on cognitive and linguistic gains, highlighting teachers' observations of improved vocabulary, pronunciation, listening skills and rhythmic coordination among c

title: Reconceptualising ‘agency in mobility’: Agency for becoming and other forms of agency in study abroad
abstract: Abstract Study‐abroad programs are increasingly adopted and supported by institutions and governments as a strategic tool for deepening internationalisation and public diplomacy through people‐to‐people, institution‐to‐institution and country‐to‐country connections. Yet, the agency of study‐abroad students who are engaged in outbound mobility as part of their study program in their home institution has long been neglected. This article draws on a study of the New Colombo Plan (NCP) to explore how Australian students exercise agency during their experiences in China. The article is based on 44 in‐depth interviews with Australian students learning abroad in China. It uses a theoretical framework combining Sen's capability approach, Marginson's notion of student self‐formation and Tran and Vu's conceptualisation of ‘agency in mobility’. The article analyses student agency in developing ethno‐relative perspectives, comparative curriculum‐specific knowledge, empathy, intercultural competence and professional skills. The research unpacks and conceptualises the five main forms of agency that Australian students exercise to navigate their experiences in China: agency for becoming, needs‐re

title: Otherwise engaged? Learning from non‐participation in research with care‐experienced students
abstract: Abstract This paper explores what can be learned when educational research “fails.” Drawing on a Welland Trust–funded project in the North East of England that aimed to support care‐experienced students transitioning from further to higher education, we reflect on why, despite sustained effort, there was a lack of engagement. We situate this “failure” within wider debates on participation and ethics in research with marginalised people. Rather than treating non‐participation as absence or dis‐engagement, we argue that it constitutes data ‐ a response that signposts to systemic, relational and methodological tensions between researchers, institutions and the communities they seek to involve. Considering research fatigue, institutional gatekeeping and top‐down assumptions within widening‐participation work and drawing on concepts of refusal, silence and relational ethics, we reposition “failure” as an opportunity for learning about how research constructs and constrains voice, agency and belonging. We conclude with implications for design and governance of future studies with care‐experienced and other seldom‐heard groups, emphasising slower timelines, genuinely co‐created processes

title: No other choice: The fracturing of reflexivity in families' pathways into (non‐)elective home education in England
abstract: Abstract In England, education is compulsory, but schooling is not: it is legal for families to home educate their children. This form of education is officially termed by the Department for Education as ‘Elective Home Education’. As this designation implies, many families home educate as a positive and preferential ‘choice’. For others, however, home education is not their desired first option. Drawing on a longitudinal research study that has explored the unfolding educational trajectories of home‐educating families, this paper focuses on parents who feel they have no other choice but to home educate to resolve broader issues their children are experiencing in secondary school. Margaret Archer's concept of ‘fractured’ reflexivity provides a novel lens for unpacking the understudied processes through which such families move involuntarily into home education. It supports understanding of the considerable distress families can endure within the school system, and how this makes it increasingly difficult for parents to construct a pathway out of the situations they find their families in. title: Chilean science teachers' conceptualisations of disability when teaching students with autism
abstract: Abstract This study examines how Chilean secondary science teachers conceptualise disability when teaching students with autism in integrated classroom settings. Grounded in critical disability studies, the research employs a qualitative story‐completion method, using a fictional classroom scenario to prompt teachers to construct narratives that reveal underlying assumptions, discourses and practices regarding disability. Data were collected from 31 in‐service science teachers (18 female; 13 male) and analysed using thematic analysis. Three interrelated themes were constructed: (a) managing regulation—the production of the ‘calm and functional’ science classroom, where disability is framed through behavioural control and participation is contingent on alignment with normative expectations; (b) teachers' positionings—how teachers' pedagogical decisions and interactions actively shape students' experiences, positioning students with autism as subjects of coordination, differentiation and, at times, surveillance; and (c) disability as a model of inspiration—where students are identified as exceptional, with inclusion often tied to displays of excellence or symbolic value. title: English teachers' journeys since the 2020 Iteration of Black Lives Matter
abstract: Abstract The 2020 resurgence of Black Lives Matter (BLM) mobilised students in England to demand greater representation of racially minoritised voices in English curriculums—a call highlighted by stark inequity: just 1.5% of GCSE texts studied are by racially minoritised authors, despite racially minoritised students comprising 38.0% of the student population. Drawing on Critical Race Theory (CRT), I investigated how 11 secondary school English teachers responded. Through thematic analysis of interview data, aided by a visual timeline stimulus, I examined both the transformative possibilities and the institutional constraints that teachers encountered. Three key findings emerged. First, BLM acted as a definitive catalyst, igniting a pedagogical desire for change. Second, change was facilitated by specific opportunities: student activism, profound engagement with new texts, diverse classrooms and examination boards' expanded offerings. Third, teachers' journeys were curtailed by systemic barriers: canon‐centric training, critical resource gaps and multifaceted institutional resistance. title: Single‐subject designs in character education: Methods for rigorous, contextual, and practitioner‐led research
abstract: Abstract Character education research is often constrained by blunt methodological tools. Surveys capture breadth without depth; case studies offer richness but lack replicability; and randomised controlled trials (RCTs), though indispensable at the policy level, are costly, disruptive and ill‐suited to everyday practice with individual pupils. More troublingly, they often invite an ergodic fallacy: assuming that what works on average must work for each individual. In reality, interventions that deliver modest positive effect sizes typically conceal a mix of no effects, negative effects and only some benefits. This leaves teachers, mentors and coaches without rigorous tools to evaluate what matters most: whether an intervention works here, now, for this pupil. This paper argues that single‐subject designs (SSDs) offer a neglected but transformative solution. SSDs involve repeated measurement in which individuals serve as their own controls, allowing stronger causal inference at the individual level compared with RCT data. They democratise research by enabling practitioners to capture and publish the wisdom of context‐sensitive practice without the machinery of large trials. Through

title: The situated professional: Preservice teachers' profiling of globally competent teachers and visions of their ‘possible professional self’
abstract: Abstract In response to globalisation, teacher education programmes worldwide are tasked with preparing globally competent teachers (GCTs). Prevailing conceptions of global competence are largely derived from Western‐centric humanistic, neoliberal and transformative narratives, creating a complex landscape for teacher identity formation. This study investigates how preservice teachers in Hong Kong, a context characterised by its unique positioning of ‘integrating nationally while engaging globally’ and a high‐stakes exam‐oriented culture, profile GCTs and envision their own ‘possible professional selves’ as GCTs. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with 18 Bachelor of Education students, the findings reveal that preservice teachers construct a hybrid and situated professional identity. They profile the GCT not as adhering to a single narrative but as a synthesis of the competing narratives. While their visions are predominantly shaped by humanistic and neoliberal narratives, limited elements of a transformative stance also emerge in concerns for educational equity. title: Effective methods for increasing levels of political self‐efficacy for girls and disadvantaged students in England
abstract: Abstract This study addresses the gap in rigorous evaluation of inclusive Citizenship Education methods in reducing gender and socioeconomic inequalities in political self‐efficacy. This article tests the effectiveness of two pedagogical approaches: counter‐narratives and think‐pair‐share. Within the context of the EU/UKRI Horizon project G‐EPIC, a quasi‐experiment was conducted with 253 Year 9 students (aged 14) recruited from 5 mixed schools across England. These schools are characterised by high levels of socioeconomic disadvantage and a significant proportion of English as an additional language. Participating students were randomly and systematically allocated into 3 groups according to age and gender, and different inclusive teaching methods were then applied in each group: (A) counter‐narrative reading, (B) counter‐narrative plus think‐pair‐share or (C) a control group. All groups then participated in a structured discussion on policies on climate change. Difference in difference (DiD) analysis was employed to test the effectiveness of the different approaches. title: Moderators' perceptions of consistency in Key Stage 2 writing moderation across local authorities
abstract: Abstract This article explores moderators’ perceptions of the consistency of Key Stage 2 (KS2) writing moderation across Local Authorities (LAs) in England, a process central to securing the reliability and fairness of teacher assessment in a high‐stakes accountability system. Drawing on survey data from 33 LA lead moderators, the study provides rare empirical insight into how moderation is reported to be enacted, interpreted and experienced at the system's local operational level. Descriptive statistics and thematic analysis indicate that, while internal consistency within LAs is perceived as strong, supported by structured training, calibration activities and established quality‐assurance procedures, significant concerns persist regarding national comparability. Respondents highlighted the interpretive complexity of the Teacher Assessment Framework, particularly the working at greater depth standard, and identified outdated exemplification materials, uneven cross‐LA collaboration and the withdrawal of external oversight by the Standards and Testing Agency as key contributors to variability. title: Middle leadership for teacher learning in China: The significance of context
abstract: Abstract A growing number of studies show the potential influence of teachers with leadership responsibilities, that is, middle leaders, on teacher learning. The study reported in this paper focused on middle leaders in China who sought to enhance teachers' capacity across various school settings. Using Hallinger's (2011) synthesised leadership for learning model, we seek to understand the relationship between school context, that is, school organisation, staff and community characteristics and middle leaders' capacity to contribute to teacher learning. We employed multi‐case studies of 18 heads of teaching‐research groups (TRGs) in English, Chinese and Mathematics from six schools with varying profiles. TRG heads are middle leaders responsible for leading teacher development by guiding practice‐based research. Without imputing causality, the analysis reveals links among variations in middle leadership and school contexts. Our analysis of interview data found that middle leaders applied contextually sensitive combinations of leadership strategies and formed different structures with teachers and principals. title: Identifying key predictors of resilience in mathematics engagement: Global evidence from PISA 2022 using machine learning
abstract: Abstract Students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds tend to show lower levels of mathematics engagement. However, some students demonstrate high mathematics engagement in the face of socioeconomic adversity. Understanding the factors that underpin such mathematics engagement resilience is crucial for advancing educational equity and quality. Drawing on the resilience framework of the Organisation for Economic Co‐operation and Development (OECD), this study investigates key personal, familial and school‐related predictors that distinguish engagement‐resilient students from their non‐resilient peers. Using the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 data from 80 economies, the analysis focuses on students in the bottom quartile of economic, social and cultural status ( N = 153,412). Three ensemble machine learning models (i.e., Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM) were employed to identify the most important predictors among 115 variables, followed by accumulated local effects analyses to examine relationships between key predictors and mathematics engagement resilience. title: A systematic review of student STEM competencies in secondary integrated STEM curricula: Recent trends, taxonomy, and challenges
abstract: Abstract Integrated STEM curricula are increasingly advocated as the technique to enhance students' STEM competencies in secondary education. However, the conceptualisation, operationalisation, assessment and challenges across current studies remain unclear. This systematic review synthesised empirical evidence on student STEM competencies in secondary integrated STEM curriculum published from 2021 to 2025. In accordance with PRISMA guidelines, 40 peer‐reviewed empirical and conceptual studies were identified across 3 databases, including Web of Science, Scopus and ERIC. These studies informed the analysis of research trends and STEM competency conceptualisation, while 31 studies were further analysed to examine reported challenges. The results indicate three key patterns: (1) recent research indicates an increasing interest in competency‐oriented integrated STEM curriculum; (2) most studies neglect to explicitly define ‘STEM competency’ as a cohesive construct; rather, they operationalise distinct skills such as engineering design and computational thinking. A taxonomy of student STEM competencies was created to synthesise these data, categorising reported competences into higher‐

title: Opportunities for learning amidst concerns of misuse: Secondary teachers' uses and perceptions of artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has a growing influence on planning, teaching and assessment practices in education. In New Zealand, the Ministry of Education (2024) has acknowledged AI's expanding role in schools; nevertheless, limited data exist on teachers' practices and perspectives regarding its implementation. To address this gap in the literature, the present study employed an online survey and thematic analysis to investigate how secondary school teachers in NZ ( N = 99) used AI tools and to examine their perceptions of these tools in educational contexts. Quantitative analysis of the survey results revealed that teachers employed AI for various practical purposes, including planning (66.7%), teaching (37.4%) and assessment (34.3%). Most respondents agreed, however, that there were limited policies (63.6%) and a lack of knowledge (59.6%) relating to AI use in schools.
