title: ‘I Am Because We Are’: An Ubuntu perspective on teacher motivation in Ghana's low‐fee private schools
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the policy paradox in Ghana's rural low‐fee private schools (LFPSs), where policies grounded in Western motivational theories threaten the sustainability of the local teaching force. Using a phenomenological case study design, we employed the indigenous Ubuntu–Nhorowondo framework to demonstrate why uncertified ‘grey area’ teachers remain profoundly motivated to teach despite precarious conditions. Drawing on virtual in‐depth interviews with 15 teachers, our analysis reveals that their motivation is not a generic psychological need but a context‐dependent duty rooted in communal survival. Critically, we expose this dynamic as a broken communal contract: the system leverages teachers' spirit of sacrifice (Ubuntu) without fulfilling its reciprocal duty to provide professional investment and care. We argue that Western motivation models fail to capture these relational drivers and propose policy recommendations that shift the focus from exploiting goodwill to building a system of mutual support, thereby creating a sustainable and equitable education pathway in developing regions.

title: Buffered and burdened agency: African students navigating Chinese higher education
abstract: Abstract China has become a major destination for African students, yet their experiences are still often framed through deficit, aid, or soft power narratives that obscure their agency. This qualitative study examines how African international students in Chinese higher education institutions exercise agency under constraint. Drawing on 16 in‐depth interviews with students from seven African countries, we used reflexive thematic analysis to explore how participants navigated academic, social, and institutional challenges. Three interlinked domains emerged: the work of learning (intensive study and language demands within opaque academic governance), belonging under negotiation (coexisting hospitality, distance, and everyday racialisation), and structures under scrutiny (scholarships, work/visa rules, pricing practices, and service visibility). Across these domains, students were not passive recipients of China–Africa ‘cooperation’ but situated actors whose efforts were patterned by China's semi‐peripheral, rule‐dense higher education ecology. Conceptually, this paper develops an agency‐under‐constraint lens that distinguishes between buffered agency—when clear rules, supportive st

title: The doctoral journey as decolonial praxis: Self‐formation of Global South students in UK higher education
abstract: Abstract Previous research concerning Global South doctoral students in the United Kingdom has mainly situated their experiences within adaptationist paradigms, emphasising cultural adjustment and assimilation into Western academic norms. Such studies often depict students as passive recipients, overlooking their agency and the transformative potential inherent in the doctoral journey. To address this gap, we draw on Paulo Freire's concept of praxis and Marginson's theory of self‐formation to explore how Global South doctoral students actively negotiate their academic journeys within the established hierarchies of Western academia. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with 22 Global South doctoral students at an elite UK university, this paper conceptualises their self‐formation as a dynamic, three‐stage process: Internalised Prestige, Reflexive Repositioning and Transformative Engagement. While students initially internalise the symbolic authority of Western academia, they gradually develop critical awareness through lived encounters with marginalisation and institutional barriers, ultimately engaging in transformative practices that challenge dominant norms and seek to reshape s

title: Biographies, ontological security and the socio‐spatial politics shaping teachers' mobility in remote Australia
abstract: Abstract The global teacher shortage continues to intensify, with disparate impacts across geographic and socio‐economic communities. In Queensland, Australia, where this study originates, post‐COVID teacher shortages have intensified workforce pressures, leaving several regional, rural and remote schools as some of the ‘hardest‐to‐staff’ in the country. Despite Queensland's mobility policy and high teacher mobility potential, encouraging teachers, especially from more metropolitan areas, to relocate to these communities has proven historically difficult. This study explores teachers' spatial and social mobility to identify determinants of individual mobility behaviour that shed new light on geographically inspired aspects of the teacher shortage. Using Vincent Kaufmann's three‐part conceptualisation of motility, we analysed semi‐structured interviews from 14 school leaders and teachers from two schools located in the very remote Northwest Queensland region. Findings revealed that teacher mobility in these contexts is shaped not only by logistical access to places, but by a complex interplay of personal motivations, values and social and professional competencies. title: The ‘problem’ of school transition and its ‘scientific’ solution: Re‐examining ECE policy through the ethics of care
abstract: Abstract In early childhood education (ECE) policy research, school transition is commonly regarded as a background for school readiness or a stable object of policy intervention, without being sufficiently associated with the ethics of care. In this article, we examine ECE policies in China and discuss how the transition from early childhood education to primary school is discursively produced as a governable ‘problem’ that entails a ‘scientific’ solution in the name of care. By adopting the ‘What is the problem represented to be?’ (WPR) approach as analytical framework, our study covers policy documents across national, provincial, prefectural and county levels. Instead of asking what should be done, we interrogate what made it possible for transition to become something that required specific action. The findings reveal that transition was framed in ECE policies as the problem of schoolification, which was regarded as a developmentally ‘inappropriate’ practice and that ‘science’ was introduced as an unquestionable ‘solution’. The prescribed ‘solution’ of ‘scientific transition’ was normalised through self‐referential policy discourse within a hierarchical administrative structur

title: Issue Information
‘…It was my choice to see how I can acquire this Western world education… and I'm happy…’: Structuration and the dialectic nature of being a Nigerian university student in the UK
abstract: Abstract This paper examines the experiences of Nigerian cross‐border students in UK higher education, focusing on how colonial legacies continue to shape the interplay between structure and agency. Three key themes emerged in the analysis of the data: First, the persistence of a ‘West is Best’ mentality reflects the internalisation of colonial hierarchies that position Western education as inherently superior while marginalising Nigerian knowledge traditions. This belief, rooted in colonial history, constrains agency by reinforcing dependency on Western epistemologies. Second, while participants described feelings of belonging, they also emphasised the need for constant adaptation and assimilation into UK academic norms. Such processes risk thinning agency by subordinating prior educational experiences and reinforcing neo‐colonial hierarchies. Third, structural misalignments in assessment practices, particularly the UK's emphasis on writing, independent research and referencing, posed challenges for students accustomed to exam‐based systems. These difficulties expose the privileging of Eurocentric academic practices and the marginalisation of alternative epistemologies. The study

title: The influence mechanism of family capital on children's academic performance in Western Chinese counties: The mediating effect of family educational investment
abstract: Abstract While the educational value of family capital has been widely acknowledged, its specific mechanisms of influence in underdeveloped regions such as counties in western China remain insufficiently examined. Drawing upon Bourdieu's theory of capital, this study conceptualized ‘family educational investment’ as a mediating variable, exploring how family capital in county‐level settings enhances children's academic performance via four dimensions of investment: economic, temporal, emotional and guidance‐oriented. Data were derived from the 2023 Western China County Child and Adolescent Development Survey, encompassing a sample of 6113 participants. Hierarchical regression analysis was conducted to assess the direct effects of family capital, and bootstrap methods were applied to examine the mediating roles of the four types of investment. The results show that family capital significantly and positively predicts children's academic achievement. Families with higher levels of capital are associated with greater investments in economic resources, time, emotional support and guidance. title: ‘Self’ and ‘othering’ as a byproduct of large‐scale assessment: An investigation into the Gaokao retake policy
abstract: Abstract While Gaokao, the National College Entrance Examination (NCEE), has been extensively discussed outside the Chinese academic circle, the retake policy of the test has not received much attention. Moreover, Gaokao research in China has predominantly examined the effectiveness of the retake decision in relation to students' demographic characteristics. Qualitative research that examines the impact of the Gaokao retake policy on the lives of test‐takers, specifically on current‐year as well as retake students, is rare. The present study aimed to fill this research gap by investigating the social impact of the Gaokao retake policy. Specifically, we examine how the impact is manifested as the discursive process of ‘self’ and ‘othering’ by current‐year and retake students. We associate Gaokao retake with global educational change to illustrate how neoliberalism in Chinese education has normalised competition, leading current‐year and retake students to the process of ‘othering’ in which self is elevated over the other, perpetuating social divisions between them. title: University strategy in transnational higher education: The strategic approaches of newly established and ‘small’ international branch campuses
abstract: Abstract Newly established international branch campuses (IBCs) commence operations without a student body, and even after several years, many institutions fail to grow beyond 500 students. Despite having unique strategic needs, small IBCs are largely overlooked in the higher education literature. This research examines the organisational‐level strategies of small IBCs, along with the push and pull factors driving their adoption. Based on data from expert informants holding senior management positions at 14 IBCs globally, as well as various secondary sources, we identified five key strategic options: pursuing growth, maintaining the status quo and transforming, selling or closing the campus. It was found that institutional growth objectives serve as a primary driver of strategic direction, with prospector‐type institutions often achieving the highest success. This paper explains the drivers behind institutions' strategic choices and discusses the implications, offering insights relevant to small higher education institutions in both international and domestic settings.

title: Opposing pathways linking gender school belonging and mathematics achievement: Evidence from PISA 2018 and 2022 in Nordic countries
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the mediating role of school belonging in the relationship between gender and mathematics achievement using data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018 and 2022 across Finland, Norway and Sweden ( N = 39,888). Structural equation modelling was employed to estimate direct and indirect associations while controlling for socioeconomic status (ESCS), with explicit comparisons conducted across countries and between the 2018 and 2022 assessment cycles. The findings reveal that gender differences in mathematics achievement are characterised by opposing pathways rather than a single directional effect. Male students report higher levels of school belonging, and school belonging is positively associated with mathematics achievement; however, the direct association between gender and achievement is negative. As a result, the positive indirect effect through belonging partially offsets the negative direct effect, leading to a non‐significant overall gender effect. title: Shaping governmentalized subjects through human capital discourse and teaching commitment in teacher professional development
abstract: Abstract Drawing on Foucault's notion of governmentality, this study investigates how teachers, as governmentalized subjects, are regulated by key factors within the context of professional development. A questionnaire was administered to all teachers in 40 randomly selected secondary schools, yielding a valid return rate of 81.06% ( n = 2966). Structural equation modelling (SEM) was then employed to test the theoretical framework underpinning the questionnaire and to identify the optimal pathways among the six constructs. The findings indicate that care of self emerges as the most influential driver of both enterprising and responsible subjectivities. Our evidence further suggests that teaching commitment and self‐improvement play a crucial role in shaping enterprising subjects, while human capital discourse serves as the determining factor in constituting responsible subjects.

title: Heterogeneity in teachers' perceptions of inclusive education and their association with school‐level indicator fulfilment
abstract: Abstract This study examined heterogeneity in teachers' perceptions of inclusive education (IE) and their association with schools' fulfilment of IE indicators in Oman. Data were collected from 430 public‐school teachers using Arabic versions of the Sentiments, Attitudes and Concerns about Inclusive Education–Revised (SACIE‐R) and a localized Inclusive Education Fulfilment Scale derived from the Pacific‐INDIE framework. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the construct validity of both measures. Latent profile analysis identified three distinct teacher profiles: Reluctant but At‐Ease (32.1%), Committed but Conflicted (28.8%) and Open and Untroubled (39.1%). Educational stage significantly predicted one pairwise profile contrast, whereas teaching experience was not significant. Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars analyses revealed significant differences in institutional fulfilment across profiles, with the Reluctant but At‐Ease group reporting significantly higher fulfilment across all 10 domains of inclusive education fulfilment, as well as on the total fulfilment score, than the Committed but Conflicted and Open and Untroubled groups. title: Flexible working and professional relationships in schools: An ecological approach
abstract: Abstract In English schools, the policy environment has recently moved considerably in favour of teachers taking planning, preparation and assessment (PPA) time away from the school site as one approach to flexible working in support of teacher retention. Adopting an ecological agency approach to agency, we argue that offsite PPA offers a lens for examining the structural conditions of teacher agency. This may support a more nuanced understanding of teacher decision‐making and teacher actions, in particular, how professional relationships influence primary teachers' use of PPA time. It draws on a reflexive thematic analysis of an online survey of school leaders ( n = 314) and semi‐structured interviews and focus groups with senior leaders ( n = 12) and teachers ( n = 21). Findings indicate that levels of professional trust, the formalisation of collaborative relationships and managerial relationships varied considerably between schools, impacting the opportunity for teachers to take their PPA time offsite. These findings offer practical insights into the complexities of offering offsite PPA in primary schools at a time of heightened political interest in flexible working. The paper

title: How do parental support profiles moderate the relationship between growth mindset on mathematics achievement? Evidence from Chinese junior high school students
abstract: Abstract A growth mindset is an important psychological resource for students' academic performance. However, its benefits are not uniform and may vary with contextual conditions, among which parental support is particularly salient. Prior research has largely focused on single dimensions of parental support, leaving limited evidence on how combinations of emotional and content support jointly shape the relationship between growth mindset and academic performance. Using data from 617 seventh‐grade students in one region of China, we assessed students' growth mindset and mathematics achievement, as well as their perceived parental emotional and content support. Latent profile analysis identified four parental support profiles: high emotional‐low content (HE‐LC), high emotional‐high content (HE‐HC), low emotional‐high content (LE‐HC) and low emotional‐low content (LE‐LC). Students in profiles characterized by high emotional support showed higher mathematics achievement than those in low‐emotional profiles, and the HE‐HC profile also exhibited the highest levels of growth mindset.
